UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate                    )
Transmission System                                                 )        Docket No. RM26-4-000


        REPLY COMMENTS OF AMERICAN TRANSMISSION COMPANY LLC


        American Transmission Company LLC, along with its corporate manager ATC

Management Inc. (collectively, “ATC”), respectfully submits the following comments in reply to

various initial comments submitted in response to the Notice Inviting Comments on the proposed

advance notice of proposed rulemaking (“proposed ANOPR”) issued by the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) in the above captioned docket,1.


I.      Reply Comments

        ATC offers limited reply comments2 to support the Commission in its decision-making

and to provide additional information on three distinct issues: ensuring flexibility through a

targeted approach, studying hybrid facilities realistically, and preserving consistent cost

allocation principles aligned with Commission and court precedent.




1
        Notice Inviting Comments, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025); Proposed ANOPR, Docket No. RM26-
4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025).

2
        Omission of a response to any comments should not be viewed by the Commission or other participants as
ATC’s endorsement of, agreement with, or acceptance of any position taken by any other participant in this
proceeding.

                                                      1
       A. Flexibility will Facilitate Timely Interconnections

        Stakeholders responding to the ANOPR consistently emphasize that speed to market has

become a critical national priority. Commenters agree that flexibility is essential to achieving

timely interconnection while maintaining grid reliability and affordability. As noted in ATC’s

initial comments,3 and echoed by several other stakeholders, efficient and expeditious

interconnection of large loads is no longer merely a commercial preference, but a matter of

national security and an economic development imperative.4


        Flexibility remains paramount. Stakeholders agree that flexibility enables creative

solutions, which are ultimately the most effective means of facilitating efficient large-load

interconnections.5 The Commission should carefully evaluate how any proposed reforms might

impact existing, and effective, processes to interconnect loads.6 A “one-size-fits-all” approach

could inadvertently hinder progress by upending established processes and increasing the risk of

implementation delays. ATC supports commenters recommending that the Commission

                                                        2
 consider adopting a policy statement or general guidance rather than a sweeping rule.7 Such an

approach would likely avoid unnecessary delays and litigation by allowing flexibility instead of

imposing rigid, binding requirements.


         Should the Commission determine that new load interconnection procedures are

necessary, requirements should be narrowly tailored to focus on experienced issues and allow

maximum flexibility. For example, the Commission should consider adopting threshold

applicability requirements based upon specific operating characteristics.8 Limiting applicability

to the subset of loads that do not meet with certain operating criteria could provide adequate

controls, ensure reliability, contain costs, while preserving the flexibility for transmission owners

such as ATC to continue to interconnect traditional, conforming loads based upon our existing

interconnection processes.9 Overall, the Commission should reinforce — rather than disrupt —

existing cost allocation principles and established business practices related to load

interconnections.

                                                           3
       B. Studying and Interconnecting Hybrid Facilities

         Initial comments reveal diverse perspectives on studying hybrid and co-located facilities.

Many stakeholders advocate for coordinated studies, while some favor serial processes and

others prefer cluster studies.10 ATC, along with other commenters, urges the Commission to

separate studies for generation and load while preserving the flexibility for local planning

authorities to rely upon their expertise to adjust sequencing and modeling.11 Imposing rigid,

nationwide requirements would risk undermining reliability and effectiveness, whereas

regionally tailored solutions ensure fair cost allocation and facilitate seamless integration into

existing interconnection processes.


         Coordinated studies raise challenges, including complex cost allocation and reliability

risks from inaccurate modeling. Generation and load are functionally different and should be

studied separately. Therefore, to the extent hybrid facilities are studied together, safeguards such




10
           See, e.g., Initial Comments of Rewiring America, Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 2 (Nov. 21, 2025) (stating
“studying large loads together with co-located generation can help identify and mitigate network constraints and
protect customers…”); Initial Comments of Engie North America, Inc., Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 3 (Nov. 21,
2025) (indicating strong support for studying co-located facilities together); Talen Initial Comments at 9 (“indicating
that “any load interconnection studies that are required should be completed on a cluster, rather than serial, basis”);
Initial Comments of Calibrant Energy Holdings LLC, Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 8 (Nov. 21, 2025) (arguing that
hybrid facilities should be studied serially); SPP Initial Comments at 19 (noting that “[s]erial interconnection studies
are preferred if the volume of requests is relatively low and one request does not impact another. However, cluster
studies may be needed if volumes become large to mitigate the time it takes to perform the studies and potential
restudies in a serial manner.”); Initial Comments of Invenergy Wind Development North America LLC, et al.,
Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 4 (Nov. 21, 2025) (“Invenergy Initial Comments”) (arguing that “load and hybrid
facilities should be studied together with generation”).
11

accounts for all impacts to the Transmission System to ensure the reliable operation of the grid”); Initial Comments

Commission to “recognize that simply assuming generation and load offset each other is insufficient and could
jeopardize reliability, affordability, and customer interests”).

                                                           4
 as process matching12 and system protection facilities must be incorporated. Misalignment

between load and generation at a shared interconnection point can lead to unintended injections

or withdrawals from the transmission system. Any injection or withdrawal must be studied,

planned for, and network upgrades must be built to avoid reliability and operational issues. As

discussed in ATC’s initial comments, transmission owners lack the necessary tools to curtail firm

service;13 therefore, the full impacts of any hybrid facility must be considered to prevent

catastrophic consequences.


       While studies must be performed separately, flexibility can increase efficiency. As the

local planning authority, ATC has unique insight into sequencing based on system details and

pending projects. ATC operates under MISO’s regional planning process and its own local

process documented in MISO’s Tariff at Attachment FF-ATCLLC, which allows ATC to

maintain flexibility in managing local transmission needs while ensuring compliance with ATC’s

service territory regulatory requirements.14 Generally, Attachment FF-ATCLLC requires ATC to

study new load interconnection requests on a first-come, first-served basis.15 However,

Attachment FF-ATCLLC offers some discretion to ATC, as the planning expert with the most

hands-on knowledge of its system and pending projects or requests, to judiciously adjust study

sequencing as needed.16 This flexibility allows ATC to engage with the planning process and

 conduct studies in an efficient manner that rigid, bright-line rules would not allow. As noted

above and in several stakeholder comments, speed to market is essential, and therefore

leveraging local expertise, along with flexibility, is vital to success.


        Finally, several commenters encourage the Commission to consider technological

solutions for large load integration, such as Grid Enhancing Technologies (GETs), Dynamic Line

Ratings (DLRs), Advanced Transmission Technologies (ATTs), advanced power electronics,

among others, to increase reliability and more efficiently interconnect large loads.17 While these

technologies can offer meaningful operational benefits, they are not substitutes for robust

transmission expansion, particularly, given the size of the loads being interconnected, with some

surpassing 1 GW. These tools can optimize existing assets, improve flexibility, and support

localized stability, but they cannot fully mitigate reliability risks posed by hybrid facilities and

large, highly variable loads. The physical scale and volatility of these new demands require both

advanced operational solutions and additional transmission capacity to maintain system integrity.

ATC supports leveraging these technologies as complementary measures within a

comprehensive planning and operations framework—not as replacements for essential

transmission infrastructure.




17

       C. Cost Allocation

        ATC, along with several stakeholders, supports continued allocation of network upgrade

costs to all transmission customers that benefit from the enhanced transmission system,

consistent with Commission precedent.18 While some commenters favor the ANOPR proposal

to directly assign 100% of network upgrade costs triggered by large load interconnections to the

load owner,19 ATC believes such direct assignment would be highly complex and likely result in

disputes, confusion, and delays. ATC agrees that large loads should bear the costs they cause;

however, the existing rolled-in rate treatment aligns with cost-causation principles and avoids

unnecessary complexity and disputes. Under Schedule 9 of MISO’s Tariff, transmission service

costs are allocated to local distribution companies based on usage through their transmission

rates and passed on to load via retail tariffs based on the service taken. Consequently, network

upgrade costs that benefit all customers are allocated according to usage, aligning with cost-

causation principles.


        As outlined in ATC’s initial comments, the Commission should provide flexibility to

preserve existing processes and cost allocation methods to avoid disputes and delays. Tight and

                                                        7
 variable timelines among load and generation projects often obscure cost responsibility for

network upgrades, increasing the likelihood of conflict. Direct assignment should be narrowly

tailored to facilities exclusively attributable to and used by new loads to help contain costs and

maintain alignment with cost-causation principles.20 In summary, ATC recommends that the

Commission avoid sweeping reforms that could lead to untenable consequences. Importantly,

any future guidance, policy statement, or rulemaking should preserve transmission owners’

ability to earn a reasonable return on transmission system investments, consistent with judicial

precedent.21 Transmission owners must continue to be compensated for the risks associated with

owning, operating, and maintaining network upgrades through mechanisms such as initial

funding under any future cost-assignment framework.


II.      Conclusion

         ATC respectfully requests that the Commission consider these limited reply comments in

any future rulemaking in this proceeding. Further, ATC continues to appreciate the willingness
